references.text: The prohibition against charging interest to poor Israelites is also mentioned in Exodus, where God commands that one should not act as a usurer toward one's brother.
Deuteronomy repeats the prohibition against charging interest to a brother but permits it toward foreigners.
Parallel legislation forbids charging interest on money, food, or anything else that can be lent out.
The psalmist describes the righteous person as one who does not lend money at interest, in accordance with the commandment in Leviticus.
Proverbs warns that whoever gathers wealth through interest and usury will ultimately have to give it to someone who is merciful toward the poor.
Ezekiel defines the righteous person as one who does not take interest or usury, thus fulfilling God's command.
Ezekiel mentions taking interest as one of the sins that lead to judgment.
The righteous son who refrains from interest and usury is praised by the prophet.
Ezekiel accuses Jerusalem of taking interest and usury, which violates the prohibition in Leviticus.
Nehemiah rebukes the rich for charging interest on their poor brothers and demands that they stop this practice in accordance with the law.
